---
description: "Use when the user hands the remaining feature lifecycle to the AI, at any stage from signed-off spec to implemented-but-unshipped; detects the stage, confirms it only when the read is not clean, and drives the rest to shipped."
---

# handover

## Scope

Triggered by `/nightshift:handover`, "hand over", "handover", "take over from here", or close conversational variants. Handover is the autonomous portion of a feature's lifecycle: it detects where the feature currently stands (shift-start below), states the read (confirming with the user only when the detection is not clean), then drives the remaining steps through to shipped. If the late-stage tail (steps 5-12) already ran in this session, handover is a no-op.

Build a single flat TaskCreate queue from the detected entry step onward before starting work; mark each step completed as its sub-skill completes and pull through to completion.

The flat handover queue is the procedure's sole normal stop authority. A nested skill's terminal integration, branch-finishing, or other end-of-skill prompt is a deferred checkpoint, not permission to stop or bypass later queued steps; continue pulling until the handover queue is empty unless this command's explicit halt conditions apply.

Accumulate user-decision-required items (`/nightshift:revise-spec` and `/nightshift:revise-plan` findings deferred for later, implementation-phase questions and out-of-scope findings, `/nightshift:revise-code` tech-debt findings) into a single "follow-up items" list maintained in a scratch file (`.tmp/handover-followups.md` in the project root), not conversation memory: long runs cross context-compaction boundaries, and the scratch file is the authoritative copy the morning report (step 12) reads and presents. Open it with a header line naming the spec and target scope so a leftover is attributable. Beneath that header, every item is exactly one canonical JSON line with this shape: `{"source":"<artifact type and identity>","sourceItemId":"<stable semantic ID>","text":"<exact item text>","proposedRoute":"<route>"}`. Every producer mints a stable semantic `sourceItemId` independent of list position, and the pair `(source, sourceItemId)` is unique. To add an item, write the complete next contents and atomically replace the scratch file. Revise transfers use the stable follow-up ID as `sourceItemId`; an existing matching pair is a successful idempotent handoff, not a duplicate or failure. The morning report decodes each JSON entry and retains its source identity when presenting it. At shift-start, a leftover copy from another artifact or an already-completed run is dead state: overwrite it without mining it; a live copy from an interrupted run on the same artifact and target scope is the resume case and keeps accumulating. Delete it only after step 12's whole tail (persistence, completion stamp, plan-removal offer) completes, so a session that dies mid-tail can re-run the tail from it.

**The unattended rule.** Handover exists so the user can walk away. Review checkpoints, whether a sub-skill's or handover's own (spec or plan review after a revise loop, the plan artifact's Spec Reconciliation per-edit approvals, follow-up triage, end-of-loop asks), are therefore deferred to the morning report rather than pausing the run mid-pipeline. Deferral, not waiver: each checkpoint becomes a follow-up item carrying what would have been asked, and the user answers it at the report in the checkpoint's own terms. Scope artifact-review checkpoints to artifacts that existed at shift start: a hardening delta is only reviewable against a baseline the user has seen, so for any artifact authored during the run (the plan when handover enters at the spec gate, and equally the code the run implements) the review pause collapses into the shipped-work summary -- report what the review run completed and changed, but do not pose the deltas as an approval question. The test is whether the review changed behavior that existed at shift start, not which artifact type it was: a fix that touches a pre-existing line without changing its behavior (a constant or helper extraction under the scout rule) does not resurrect the checkpoint, while a fix that alters pre-existing behavior does. A corollary: workflow-instruction files (nightshift plugin files, the user's global CLAUDE.md, memory files) are not edited mid-run, whether the impulse comes from `/nightshift:revise-lore` or from a revise loop's dimension or authoring retrospective (whose own "apply with the user's approval" instruction is one of the deferred asks, never an auto-pass); every candidate edit to them becomes a follow-up item (the concrete edit plus the session evidence motivating it), applied only after morning-report approval via the persistence mechanics in step 12. Applying instruction changes mid-run would skip the user's review of text that governs future runs and let a session-local workaround mask a defect in the instructions. The corollary is about lore, not target work: when the plugin repo itself is the project being handed over (self-hosting), its files are the implementation surface and the pipeline edits them normally. The run still stops at the shift-start confirm line where detection raises one (a clean detection proceeds on the stated read), for destructive, irreversible, or outward-facing actions, and when work is genuinely blocked on missing input. Brainstorming sign-off keeps its normal interactive flow, because producing an approved design is the human's work and handover never starts below it.

## Artifact locations and selection

Handover looks for specs and plans in the project's established locations; when a project has none, the standard fallback is `.claude/specs/` for specs and `.claude/plans/` for plans.

When multiple candidate files coexist (stale plans persist because removal is only offered, never forced), select the artifact for the feature under discussion using the same resolution order the revise skill's scope rules use: the artifact named or implied by the invocation and conversation context first, then the most recently modified candidate, with `git status` recency as tiebreaker where the candidates are tracked (untracked candidates, ignored or simply new, fall back to file modification time alone). The confirm line names the chosen file paths explicitly, so a wrong pick is visible before any work starts. Handover operates on one in-flight feature per invocation; coexisting artifacts are disambiguated here, not orchestrated in parallel.

## Backlog entries count as specs

The spec role is filled by a dedicated spec file when one exists; otherwise by the backlog entry or entries whose text carries the design (a feature entry and its breakout file especially, but bug and quick-win entries too when their text is the design record). "Spec" throughout this command means whichever artifact fills that role.

Stamp targets and completion recording follow the form. A spec file takes hardening stamps and the step-12 completion stamp as written. When the entry has a breakout file (`features/<slug>.md`, `bugs/<slug>.md`), that file is the stamp target: revise-spec hardening stamps and the step-12 completion stamp land there exactly as on a spec file, and the file's persistence after shipping makes the stamps durable. Index-only entries take no stamps: per-entry stamps inside a shared index defeat the file-scoped fingerprint and clutter the scannable backlog; their completion record is the walk-and-remove archive move (gone from the active index, present in the history archive), and their currency check is the shift-start validation below. At step 12, backlog-entry-specced work with no breakout file skips the stamp with a one-line note.

## Shift-start: stage detection

**Target scope first.** Before walking the ladder, resolve which feature and which scope this handover takes over: from the invocation, then session context, then the spec's own phasing declaration (a phased spec names its feature phases and the sections each covers), and, when none of those establish it, by asking the user. A spec with no phasing declaration defaults to `whole file`, so the ask is reserved for genuinely phased or ambiguous cases. A feature phase is handover's conversational term for a stamp-comparable implementation scope; a revise review round or wave is an internal repeated-review unit and does not alter that target scope.

**Coverage** is containment plus currency: a stamp covers the target scope when its recorded scope contains it AND the artifact's in-scope content is unchanged since the stamp (the artifact-drift check below supplies the currency signal; drift that cannot be localized to sections counts as in-scope). Drift within the target scope defeats coverage outright, and the ladder treats the artifact as not hardened (or not completed) for that scope; this is a rung decision, not a soft flag, though the user's confirm-line answer still overrides.

**Validate before proceeding.** Between resolving the artifacts and the stated conclusion, dispatch one fresh agent to validate the governing spec (or backlog entries) and plan against the current repo: does the described problem, design, and every file reference still hold? Stamps prove a hardening loop ran when the stamp was written; this validates content against today's tree, and for backlog-entry specs, which carry no stamps, it is the only currency check available. Fold the findings into the stated conclusion; validation findings are one of the signals that downgrade a clean detection into a confirm-first one. The validation agent also reports any surviving `(live-claim: ...)` markers anywhere in the governing spec, whatever rung detection lands on; they surface in the stated conclusion as a flag with the claim's context, and the user rules on them there (probe now, defer knowingly by rewriting to `(live-claim: deferred <date>)`, or proceed leaving the flag standing), since work may have outrun unprobed claims. A probe run here follows step 1's rules, including the contradicting-probe three-way split. `probed` and `deferred` markers surface as a note, not a flag; only `provisional` downgrades a clean detection. This flag is deliberately the mechanism's only resume-time detection: detection never re-enters probing on account of the markers themselves (a not-hardened spec still routes through step 1, probes included). The validation agent also checks the governing spec for a complete `Operating context` section (absent vs skeletal per the revise-spec grounding step) and reports an absent or skeletal section as a flag. That flag downgrades a clean detection to confirm-first, and is resolved by the entry-point consult: the user, present at shift start, fills or approves the section before any unattended continuation proceeds (the spec's grounding step derives it, consulting this same user).

Walk the ladder top-down and enter the procedure at the first rung whose condition holds. State the conclusion in one line, naming the chosen spec/plan paths, the target scope, and any stamp or staleness details, for example: "Spec .claude/specs/foo.md hardened for sections 3-5 (stamped 2026-07-04 09:41 at a1b2c3d), matching the target scope; no plan found; taking over from planning." When the detection is clean (the rung decided on solid evidence, artifact selection unambiguous, validation found no issues, and no staleness, drift, live-claim, or inconclusive-evidence flags are raised), proceed directly to building the task queue: the stated conclusion is the user's interrupt point, not a question. Any flag, ambiguity, or validation finding instead asks the user to confirm before work starts ("... Correct?"), and the user's answer always overrides inference. References to "the confirm line" throughout this command mean this stated conclusion; where a flag applies, it is posed as the question just described.

Throughout the ladder, "same-session evidence" means the event demonstrably happened earlier in the current conversation. Where evidence is inconclusive, the rung reads as not satisfied (a failed check is not a clean check), and the confirm line states which question could not be answered, in that rung's own terms.

1. **Late-stage tail already ran this session**: no-op; say so.
2. **Spec carries a completion stamp covering the target scope** (containment plus currency, per the coverage definition above): the work already shipped; report that and stop, unless the user indicates a further scope is intended (which re-enters the ladder for it).
3. **Implementation complete**: the plan's tasks are committed. Commits are deliberately not labeled with plan-task numbers (plan hygiene forbids it), so the evidence is correspondence between plan-named files and commits since the plan's hardening stamp, or same-session evidence; inconclusive reads as not complete. A history rewrite breaks this evidence entirely (the stamp SHA is no longer an ancestor of HEAD); the confirm line must then say outright that handover cannot tell whether the implementation already landed, since the ladder would otherwise propose re-implementation at rung 4. If complete: enter at step 5 (the late-stage tail).
4. **Plan exists.** Hardened (stamp or same-session evidence): enter at step 4 (implementation). Not hardened: enter at step 3 (revise-plan).
5. **Signed-off spec exists** (see Sign-off marker below). Hardened for the target scope (coverage, per the definition above): enter at step 2 (planning). Not hardened: enter at step 1 (the spec gate). Currency is what makes the feature-phase rule work: a whole-file stamp from an earlier feature phase contains later sections by grammar, but sections added or edited after that stamp fail currency, which is exactly what mandates re-hardening for a later feature phase.
6. **No signed-off spec**: halt and direct the user to the brainstorming skill. Producing specs is the human's work by design. When sign-off is merely undeterminable (as opposed to determinably absent), ask the user rather than halting.

## Sign-off marker

A spec is signed off when the user has approved the design. The durable marker is a `Status: signed off <date and time>, content: <fingerprint>` line in the spec's header (fingerprint per the recipe below). Handover is the marker's only writer, and writes it lazily: at shift-start, sign-off is established by the marker, by same-session evidence of the approval, or by asking the user; whenever it is established and the line is absent, write it so future sessions have the signal. Approval itself happens in the brainstorming flow, which this plugin deliberately does not modify, so lazy first-contact writing is the normal path, not a migration special case.

## Provenance stamps

Completed spec and plan review runs append hardening stamps (see the post-loop steps in the revise skill's `spec.md` / `plan.md`); the persisted stamp token remains `graduated`, and handover writes the completion stamp at step 12. All stamps live under a `## Hardening` section at the end of the artifact, created if absent:

```
- revise-spec graduated 2026-07-05 14:32 at a1b2c3d, scope: sections 3-5, content: 9f3a2b1c
- handover completed 2026-07-06 09:15 at e4f5a6b, scope: sections 3-5, content: 1c2d3e4f
```

- **Scope grammar**: `scope: whole file` for a whole-file pass, or `scope: sections <headings or ranges>` for a section-scoped pass. Plans are typically hardened whole-file. Rung comparisons are scope against scope, one grammar everywhere.
- **The SHA** is the repo HEAD commit at write time. The hardening edits themselves are uncommitted at stamp time, so a hardening stamp's SHA is the pre-hardening baseline; the artifact file itself is therefore always excluded from any SHA-based overlap diff (it would otherwise self-flag its own hardening edits), and edits to the artifact are instead owned by the fingerprint-based drift check below.
- **The fingerprint** is a short hash of the artifact's design content, excluding provenance lines (the `## Hardening` section and the `Status:` header). Canonical recipe, run from the repo root:

  ```bash
  awk '/^## Hardening$/{exit} !/^Status:/' <artifact-path> | sha256sum | cut -c1-8
  ```

  The fingerprint, not any timestamp, is the drift signal: it is machine-independent (clones and sync tools rewrite modification times) and inherently blind to the workflow's own stamp appends and the `Status:` sign-off line. Inline markers such as `(live-claim: ...)` are body content and DO move the fingerprint; see Post-stamp edits below. Likewise, writing or editing the `Status:` sign-off marker shifts the content: the recipe excludes the `Status:` line itself but not the blank lines placed around it, so after writing the marker recompute the fingerprint (record the post-marker digest in the marker's own `content:` field) and refresh the covering hardening stamp per Post-stamp edits. Timestamps in stamps serve the age check and latest-provenance ordering only.
- **Post-stamp edits**: when a sanctioned pipeline step edits a stamped artifact after its stamp (any live-claim marker rewrite, whichever step performs it: step 1's fold-back, a shift-start disposition the user requests, step 6's rewrite, a step-12 disposition; plus revise-plan's Spec Reconciliation), append a fresh stamp line matching the scope of the graduated stamp it refreshes (one refreshed line per affected graduated stamp on phased specs), the current HEAD, and the new fingerprint, suffixed with the reason in parentheses, e.g. `- revise-spec refreshed 2026-08-02 17:20 at 1a2b3c4, scope: whole file, content: 9d8c7b6a (live-claim fold-back)`. The prefix names the artifact's hardening loop, whichever step performs the refresh. A `refreshed` line supplies the fingerprint for the drift check only: the age check and the content-overlap check continue to baseline on the most recent `graduated` stamp, and the sign-off baseline is deliberately not advanced (a refresh restores hardening coverage, nothing more). A marker-only rewrite therefore still trips the sign-off drift check on the next resume; that re-confirmation is expected and cheap, not a defect. Without the refresh, the drift rule correctly reads the artifact as no longer covered and forces a full re-hardening the sanctioned edit does not warrant. On an index-only backlog entry, which takes no stamps, skip the refresh with a one-line note.
- **Migration**: artifacts hardened before stamps existed carry none; detection treats them as not hardened and the confirm line is the correction point (self-healing: any future completed spec or plan review appends its stamp). A stamp that is present but lacks a `content:` fingerprint (hand-edited or malformed) is treated the same way for currency: not current, fail closed, surfaced in the confirm line.

## Staleness sanity check

When a detection rung rests on a stamp, sanity-check it before trusting it:

- **Age**: flag if the stamp is more than 48 hours old, baselining on the most recent `graduated` stamp (`refreshed` lines do not reset the clock, per Post-stamp edits). Hardening normally immediately precedes planning or implementation; anything older deserves a look. The number is a deliberate default guideline, not a gate.
- **Content overlap**: list files changed since the stamp commit (`git diff --name-only <sha>..HEAD`, excluding the artifact itself) and judge whether any are in the vicinity of the artifact's subject matter. A plan names its files explicitly; for a spec, infer the affected areas from the stamped scope. Unrelated churn passes silently. There is deliberately no commit-count threshold; relatedness is the signal, not volume.
- **Artifact drift**: compare the artifact's current content fingerprint against the recorded one. For hardening or completion currency, compare against the most recent covering stamp; for sign-off currency, the baseline is the marker, advanced only by a later whole-file handover completion stamp, whose morning-report sign-off re-approved the design and whose fingerprint becomes the new baseline. A section-scoped completion stamp does not advance it: a whole-file fingerprint cannot tell scope-limited re-approval apart from unapproved edits, so on a mismatch fail closed and re-confirm sign-off at the confirm line. A hardening stamp never advances the baseline; re-hardening is not approval. For section-scoped targets, true drift must additionally be localized: diff the artifact's current content against its content at the commit that introduced the stamp line (the post-hardening baseline; never baseline on the recorded time, which unavoidably predates the commit that carries it), and map the changed lines to sections. Drift within the target scope defeats coverage at the rung level; drift demonstrably elsewhere is a soft flag; drift that cannot be localized (untracked artifacts, unusable history) is treated as in-scope, fail closed, and the confirm line says so. Sign-off approval covers the whole design; only a whole-file completion stamp renews it.
- **Degraded mode**: the overlap diff is only meaningful when the stamp SHA is an ancestor of HEAD. After a rebase, squash, or on a machine that never had the commit, it is not; the overlap check is then inconclusive and reported as such, never silently treated as clean. The same ancestry break invalidates rung 3's implementation-completeness evidence; rung 3 owns how that surfaces.

The age flag, the overlap check, and out-of-scope drift are soft judgment calls, never hard gates; they surface in the confirm line together with an offer: (a) quick validity check (one fresh agent reads the artifact against the current repo state and reports whether it still holds), (b) full re-run of the scoped revise loop, (c) proceed as-is. Sign-off drift (a mismatch against the sign-off baseline per the artifact-drift rule above) carries one extra requirement: re-confirming sign-off with the user (refreshing the marker) before proceeding, since neither a validity check nor re-hardening substitutes for approval.

## Version-control-optional artifacts

Specs, plans, and backlog files may be git-ignored by user election; the `.gitignore` is the election, checked per file (`git check-ignore`, tracked status). Never attempt to commit an ignored artifact (write the edit, skip the commit with at most a one-line note). When an ignore entry matches a still-tracked file, the ignore entry wins as the statement of intent; note once that the untracking is incomplete and suggest `git rm --cached`. Git-based recency evidence applies only to tracked artifacts; untracked ones use file modification time (selection tiebreak only; nothing load-bearing).

## Triage during revise rounds

If a finding changes the implementation scope (what we're building, not how we describe it), block and ask: that's a brainstorm gap that needs resolving before code lands. This block survives the unattended rule as genuinely blocked work: halt the run rather than implementing all night past an unresolved design gap or silently deferring it. Polish-shaped findings (clarity, naming, missing context) go to the follow-up list and the loop continues.

## Procedure

1. **Spec gate.** `/nightshift:revise-spec` scoped to the target scope, run to completion under the skill's review rules. Handover's own review pause on the hardened spec (a checkpoint of this command, not of the revise skill) is deferred per the unattended rule: the noteworthy hardening deltas become a morning-report item. Keeping this step ahead of planning puts the natural context-compaction boundary here: run it at the brainstorm tail while the design context is warm, then compact, and a fresh handover session starts directly at planning with the spec already hardened. Findings flow into the follow-up items list. **Live-claim verification** closes the gate: when the hardened spec carries `(live-claim: provisional)` markers (written by revise-spec's Design-soundness criterion on repo-unverifiable runtime claims), probe each one against the live system in every distinct context the feature covers, using whatever tooling the session has (browser automation, API access), and fold the results back before planning begins: a confirming probe rewrites the marker to `(live-claim: probed <date>)`. A contradicting probe splits three ways: a correction local to the spec's record is an inline edit plus stamp refresh; a design-affecting correction re-enters the spec gate; a contradiction that invalidates a design decision halts per the triage rule above. Probes are observation-only; a claim whose only probe would mutate outward state is carried forward as provisional with a morning-report checkpoint item naming the blocked probe (the unattended rule's halt stays reserved for unsettled claims that block the design itself, per the triage rule above). When the environment cannot reach the live system, carry the claims forward explicitly as provisional and ensure step 6's end-to-end verification covers each one. A claim whose probe requires an artifact this run cannot produce is unreachable by construction rather than merely unreached (behavior that appears only in a released or installed build, when release is user-gated at the morning report): it stays provisional through step 6 without counting as a skipped verification, and its morning-report item names the release as the probe's precondition, so step 12's disposition is recorded as a knowing `deferred <date>` rather than reading as an unprobed gap; step 6 still names such a claim, and naming it satisfies coverage without resolving it. Where a placement or design choice would retire the claim outright instead of deferring it, prefer that: an unprobeable dependency avoided is worth more than one carefully tracked. Fold-back edits change the artifact after its hardening stamp: refresh the stamp per Provenance stamps.
2. **Write the implementation plan** via the `superpowers:writing-plans` skill.
3. `/nightshift:revise-plan`: run to completion under the skill's review rules. Its Spec Reconciliation step applies spec-worthy corrections directly; the unattended rule defers the per-edit approvals, so record each applied correction as a checkpoint item for the morning report.
4. **Implement the plan** using the `superpowers:subagent-driven-development` skill. One fresh subagent per plan task; dispatch in parallel where the dependency graph allows. Verify each batch's commits landed on the intended branch: a subagent that inherits a git-worktree skill may create a worktree and commit on a separate branch even when told to work on the current one, so check `git log` after each batch rather than assuming. Use subagents even when the plan contains complete verbatim code: dispatch keeps implementation churn (file contents, test output) out of the controller's context window, which is a primary benefit on its own, separate from the fresh-context review. On projects that track the plan file in git, revise-plan's uncommitted hardening stamp dirties the working tree throughout implementation: keep the plan file out of every implementation commit. When the plan is later removed (per the step-12 offer, or a plan task that prescribes its own cleanup), plain `git rm` refuses the stamp-modified file; use `git rm -f`. The committed deletion loses nothing: git history keeps the plan retrievable, and a landed plan left in the working tree reads as in-flight work to stage detection.
5. `/nightshift:revise-code`: run to completion under the skill's review rules. Valid-but-deferred findings flow into the follow-up items list across all rounds; do not prompt on them at end-of-loop.
6. **Verify end-to-end.** Drive the affected flow in the running app or tool and observe the behavior (the `verify` skill's discipline, if that skill is available: exercise the change, don't just trust tests or typecheck). Skip with a one-line note when the session's diff has no runtime surface to drive (docs-only or test-only changes). Where the run settles any claim still marked `(live-claim: provisional)`, whatever step first surfaced it, rewrite its marker to `(live-claim: probed <date>)` on a confirming result and refresh the stamp per Provenance stamps; a contradicting result routes per step 1's three-way split, never to a marker rewrite.
7. `/nightshift:revise-docs`: update project docs to reflect what shipped.
8. **Backlog bookkeeping check.** In projects with the four-index `.claude/` layout, confirm the shipping protocol ran for everything that landed this session: history-archive entries appended (`FEATURES_HISTORY.md` / `BUGS_HISTORY.md` / `QUICK_WINS_HISTORY.md`), slice bullets struck through and the parent's top-level `**Requires:**` line advanced where a slice shipped, and the walk-and-remove sweep applied to every other `**Requires:**` line in `FEATURES.md` / `BUGS.md`. `/nightshift:revise-docs`' Completed-features guideline owns the protocol; this step exists as an explicit checkpoint because `/nightshift:ready`'s correctness depends on the sweep having run. Skip with a one-line note in projects without the layout.
9. `/nightshift:revise-lore`: review the session for CLAUDE.md / plugin updates worth persisting. Project-repo lore (the project's CLAUDE.md, backlog pattern notes) may be applied and committed directly; it is itemized in the morning report's lore-outcomes section. Workflow-instruction lore (nightshift plugin files, the global CLAUDE.md, memory files) is not applied here, per the unattended rule's corollary: draft each candidate as a follow-up item, and run revise-lore's fresh-eyes pass over the full set of drafted workflow-instruction diffs, including those proposed by earlier steps' dimension and authoring retrospectives, before the morning report presents them, so the user reviews vetted proposals.
10. **Persist workflow edits.** A pointer, not work: approved plugin follow-ups are applied inside step 12's post-triage tail, never earlier. The step stays in the queue so a resumed session sees persistence as part of the pipeline; mark it completed together with step 12.
11. **Full test suite.** Run the project's full test suite as defined in the project's CLAUDE.md. This phrase is the explicit ask that overrides any per-project "never run the full suite without filter" rule. If the suite is not green, halt and surface failures before triage; test failures are not follow-up items.
12. **Morning report.** Open with the shipped-work summary and verification outcome, then two sections that are easy to omit and must not be: **lore outcomes** (the session's whole lore ledger: project-repo lore applied directly, with commit ids, plus every drafted workflow-instruction proposal awaiting triage, whichever step proposed it; retrospective-proposed plugin edits live here, not in the next section) and **retrospective outcomes** (each revise loop's dimension- and authoring-retrospective outcomes, explicitly including null results like "no prompt changes warranted" or "no habit worth promoting", pointing at lore outcomes for any edits either proposed; a silent retrospective is indistinguishable from a skipped one). Then surface the accumulated follow-up items (from all prior steps) with a default route proposed for each: (a) fix now (small, scout-rule, low-risk), (b) track, (c) skip. Two shapes need their own terms: deferred review checkpoints are asked as the question they carry (approve, adjust, revert), not forced into fix/track/skip; and a route-(b) item tracks in its own home: the handed-over project's `QUICK_WINS.md` for project items, and for workflow-lore items the plugin repo's own tracking (its backlog if one exists; otherwise ask at triage where to put it).

    Presentation mechanics. The user saw none of the churn behind the list, so present items strictly one at a time: one item per message, rendered as a self-contained dialog whose question text carries the background needed to decide in isolation (where the item came from, what changed since, the exact proposed edit) plus the recommended action, then stop the turn and wait for the user's decision before presenting the next item. Never batch the remaining items into one message, even as a numbered summary with per-item recommendations and a bulk-approve escape hatch; the sequential ask IS the review surface, and a batched list forces the user to either rubber-stamp or re-request the per-item flow (observed 2026-08-02: a batched morning report had to be re-run item by item on request). The dialog (AskUserQuestion or the harness equivalent) presents the routes as options carrying per-option consequence descriptions, the recommended route first; everything the user needs goes inside the dialog because text placed before a dialog in the same turn may not render. Fall back to plain prose plus a text question only when an item's background genuinely exceeds what the dialog can carry. This mechanics rule supersedes the revise skill's bulk-approval ask for the morning report only; standalone revise runs keep bulk-approve, since their user is present and holds the loop's context.

    Plugin follow-ups approved here are applied with release provenance: edit the plugin repo clone (not the installed cache), bump the plugin version once per unpushed batch, commit in the clone, and leave pushing to the user unless directed. Approved global-CLAUDE.md and memory edits are persisted via whatever mechanism backs each file; for gist-backed files, flag the local-vs-gist divergence so the user can sync.

    After triage completes, everything is verified, and the user has signed off: report any surviving `(live-claim: provisional)` markers and record the user's disposition for each in the marker itself (`probed <date>` if the run settled it, `deferred <date>` on a knowing deferral, so the ruling survives the conversation and the completion stamp is never written over silently-unprobed claims), then append the completion stamp to the spec (format and fingerprint per Provenance stamps above; write it BEFORE the next offer, so a session that dies in between leaves the plan in place and the next handover merely re-runs the tail, wasteful but safe), then offer to remove the plan file (plans are ephemeral scaffolding once work lands; the spec stays). Re-entry after any partial run re-runs the whole detected stage; sub-step resume is deliberately not tracked across sessions.
